request_text:
Stand up a focused collection effort targeting Mexico-based TCOs—specifically the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG)—to detect and monitor anticipated adaptive shifts in drug smuggling techniques, routing methodologies, and operational tradecraft that are expected to emerge in direct response to the heightened U.S. security posture currently being maintained along the southwest border region. This effort is grounded in the findings of the 2025 threat assessment, which has conclusively identified official ports of entry (POEs) as the primary smuggling vector for fentanyl and other synthetic narcotics, with concealment methods predominantly involving passenger vehicles and commercial tractor trailers transiting through these legitimate crossing points. However, given the increased enforcement pressure, the intelligence community anticipates that these transnational criminal organizations will seek to adapt their tradecraft, at least on a temporary basis, to circumvent the strengthened security measures now in place.

The rationale for this collection effort is straightforward: historically, TCOs have demonstrated significant operational agility in response to law enforcement and border security pressure. When one vector becomes higher-risk due to interdiction efforts, these organizations have consistently shown a willingness and capability to diversify their smuggling approaches. This pattern of adaptive behavior necessitates proactive intelligence collection rather than reactive analysis after new methods have already been established and operationalized.

To this end, I am formally requesting HUMINT and SIGINT tasking nominations to be submitted through the established National Collection Coordination process. The primary intelligence objective of these nominations should be the detection of early indicators and warning signals of route diversification by the targeted TCOs. Specifically, the collection effort should be designed to identify whether these organizations are pivoting toward increased utilization of unofficial border crossings—sometimes referred to as "between the ports" crossings through remote desert or rural terrain—as well as any expansion of maritime smuggling approaches along either the Pacific or Gulf coast corridors, or any renewed or increased investment in cross-border tunneling activity, which has historically been a significant concern in urban areas along the border such as the Tijuana-San Diego and Nogales corridors.

It is essential that these tasking nominations be carefully coordinated with the Drug Enforcement Administration's Special Operations Division (DEA SOD) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) intelligence components to ensure thorough deconfliction. This coordination step is critical not only to avoid duplication of effort across the intelligence and law enforcement communities but also to protect the integrity of any existing operations, sources, and methods that may already be directed against these same targets. Deconfliction failures in the past have occasionally resulted in compromised operations or endangered sources, so this requirement should be treated with the utmost seriousness and diligence throughout the nomination and approval process.

Furthermore, all tasking nominations must explicitly reference and align with the existing National Intelligence Priorities Framework (NIPF) priority designations for counternarcotics. This alignment ensures that our collection requests are properly prioritized within the broader national intelligence enterprise and that they receive appropriate resource allocation and attention from the collecting agencies. Any nominations that fail to reference the applicable NIPF priority frameworks may face delays in processing or may not receive adequate prioritization, so drafters should ensure this linkage is clearly articulated in the nomination documentation.

In addition to the primary focus on smuggling route and technique adaptation, this collection effort must also incorporate a dedicated reporting stream to capture and analyze changes in precursor chemical sourcing patterns. Specifically, we need periodic intelligence reporting that monitors the supply chain dynamics involving People's Republic of China (PRC)-based chemical suppliers who provide the precursor chemicals that feed into Mexican fentanyl production laboratories. The PRC-based precursor supply chain has been identified as a critical upstream vulnerability in the fentanyl production cycle, and any shifts in sourcing patterns—whether involving new supplier networks, alternative chemical precursors designed to evade regulatory controls, changes in shipping routes or transshipment points, or modifications to financial transaction methods used to pay for these precursors—could provide valuable early warning of broader changes in TCO production capabilities and intentions. This periodic reporting should be structured to enable trend analysis over time and should be made available to all relevant interagency partners working the counternarcotics mission.

Regarding the timeline for this effort, I need the initial tasking nominations to be fully drafted, reviewed internally, and routed through the appropriate approval channels no later than the end of next week. This deadline is firm because we have a commitment to brief the interagency working group on this collection effort and its initial findings or status the following Monday. The briefing will need to convey not only the scope and objectives of the collection effort but also the status of the tasking nominations and any preliminary coordination outcomes with DEA SOD and CBP intelligence. Meeting this timeline will demonstrate the urgency and seriousness with which we are approaching this intelligence gap and will help secure the buy-in and support of interagency partners who will be critical to the success of this collection endeavor.

All personnel involved in drafting and routing these nominations should treat this as a high-priority tasking and allocate their time accordingly to meet the established deadline.

request_text:
Establish a comprehensive, enduring collection plan to monitor China's commercial space sector trajectory and its potential dual-use implications for PLA space-based intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) as well as satellite communications (satcom) capabilities. This collection plan must be designed as a sustained, long-term intelligence effort rather than a one-time assessment, reflecting the dynamic and rapidly evolving nature of China's space enterprise and the strategic importance of maintaining persistent awareness of developments across this domain.

A central priority of this collection effort is the identification and detailed mapping of which international partners Beijing is actively courting, engaging, or has already secured for its International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) initiative, which represents a deliberate strategic alternative to the U.S.-led Artemis Accords framework. Understanding the diplomatic, technological, and financial dimensions of these partnerships is critical, as they may reveal broader geopolitical alignment patterns, technology-sharing arrangements, and potential vectors through which dual-use space technologies could proliferate to nations outside traditional Western alliance structures. The plan should seek to identify not only which nations have signed memoranda of understanding or formal agreements, but also which are in earlier stages of engagement, including preliminary discussions, joint feasibility studies, or personnel exchanges related to lunar exploration cooperation.

The collection plan should leverage the full spectrum of available intelligence disciplines, including but not limited to open-source intelligence (OSINT), signals intelligence (SIGINT), and geospatial intelligence (GEOINT), in order to construct a detailed and continuously updated picture of the commercial-military nexus that characterizes China's space enterprise. This nexus is of particular concern because China's civil-military fusion strategy deliberately blurs the lines between ostensibly commercial space entities and organizations that directly or indirectly support PLA modernization objectives. The plan must therefore be designed to identify, track, and assess entities that may present themselves as purely commercial ventures but that in reality serve as procurement fronts, technology development platforms, or operational adjuncts for PLA space capabilities.

Specific collection targets and lines of effort should include, but are not limited to, the following areas:

First, tracking China's launch cadence across all launch providers—both established state-owned enterprises such as the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) and the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), as well as the growing number of nominally private or commercial launch companies such as Galactic Energy, LandSpace, iSpace, and others. Understanding launch tempo, success rates, payload types, and orbital insertion parameters is essential for assessing the overall maturation and capacity of China's space launch infrastructure.

Second, monitoring orbital deployments with sufficient granularity to characterize the purpose, capability, and operational status of satellites and other space objects placed into orbit by Chinese entities. This includes tracking the build-out of large constellations for communications, remote sensing, and navigation, as well as identifying any deployments that may have counterspace, co-orbital inspection, or other militarily significant functions.

Third, mapping the expansion of ground infrastructure, including new launch facilities, tracking and telemetry stations, mission control centers, satellite operations facilities, and ground-based space surveillance assets. This ground infrastructure mapping should extend to overseas facilities and agreements that China may be establishing with partner nations, as these can provide critical insights into the global reach and redundancy of China's space operations architecture.

Fourth, identifying and characterizing any technology transfer arrangements between China and partner nations, whether these take the form of formal government-to-government agreements, commercial joint ventures, academic collaborations, or less formal channels of technology exchange. Understanding the nature, scope, and direction of technology flows is essential for assessing proliferation risks and for identifying potential leverage points or vulnerabilities in China's international space partnerships.

The collection plan should be structured to produce quarterly deliverables that provide updated assessments across all lines of effort, enabling policymakers and operational planners to maintain current awareness of trends, developments, and emerging issues. These quarterly products should be designed to be cumulative, building upon previous reporting to create an increasingly detailed and nuanced understanding of China's space enterprise over time. Each quarterly deliverable should highlight significant changes, new developments, and shifts in assessed trajectories since the previous reporting period.

However, prior to the establishment of the regular quarterly reporting cadence, an initial baseline assessment must be delivered within a two-week timeline. This baseline assessment is intended to provide a comprehensive foundation upon which all subsequent collection and analysis will build, and it must cover the entirety of China's space modernization trajectory through the year 2030. The scope of this initial baseline must span all relevant technology sub-domains, specifically including: crewed spaceflight programs (including the Chinese Space Station and any future crewed lunar or deep-space ambitions); positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) constellations (primarily BeiDou and any augmentation or next-generation systems); commercial launch providers (both established and emerging); ISR architecture (including electro-optical, synthetic aperture radar, electronic intelligence, and other remote sensing satellite systems); and counterspace programs (encompassing kinetic and non-kinetic anti-satellite capabilities, co-orbital threats, directed energy research, electronic warfare capabilities targeting space systems, and cyber threats to space infrastructure).

Throughout all products—both the initial baseline and subsequent quarterly deliverables—the assessment should reflect best-efforts analytic confidence levels. This means that each key judgment, finding, or projection should be accompanied by an explicit statement of the level of confidence the analytic team holds in that assessment, along with a brief explanation of the factors supporting or limiting that confidence, such as the volume and quality of available sourcing, the degree of corroboration across intelligence disciplines, and the inherent uncertainty associated with projecting future developments. This transparency regarding analytic confidence is essential for enabling consumers of the intelligence to appropriately calibrate their decision-making based on the assessed reliability of the information provided.

Finally, the collection planning team must proactively coordinate with existing equities at the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) to ensure that this effort complements rather than duplicates ongoing collection and analytic activities. This coordination should be designed to achieve two objectives simultaneously: first, avoiding unnecessary redundancy and ensuring efficient use of limited collection and analytic resources across the intelligence community; and second, ensuring that there are no seams or gaps in coverage, particularly with respect to emerging commercial entities that may not yet be well-known or well-characterized within existing intelligence frameworks but that may serve as PLA procurement fronts or dual-use technology development platforms. The coordination mechanism should include regular information-sharing sessions, deconfliction of collection tasking, and collaborative analysis where appropriate, in order to maximize the collective intelligence community's understanding of China's space enterprise while minimizing duplication of effort.

request_text:
Stand up comprehensive collection requirement targeting Mexico-based TCOs—specifically the Sinaloa Cartel and the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG)—with a particular and sustained focus on their fentanyl and synthetic opioid production capabilities, manufacturing infrastructure, and trafficking pipelines directed into the United States. This tasking is driven by the ongoing national security and public health crisis posed by synthetic opioids, which have been the primary driver of overdose fatalities in the U.S. for several years running, and by the need to understand whether recent positive trends in fatality data reflect genuine operational disruption of supply networks or are attributable to other intervening factors on the demand side.

The requirement should establish multiple collection threads organized around the following priority areas:

**1. Smuggling Methodologies at Southwest Border Ports of Entry:**
The primary collection priority should be intelligence on smuggling methodologies employed at official ports of entry (POEs) along the entire U.S.-Mexico southwest border, spanning California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. This includes, but is not limited to, detailed reporting on concealment techniques utilized in passenger vehicles—such as aftermarket compartments, fuel tank modifications, dashboard voids, and seat cavity concealment—as well as concealment methods employed in commercial tractor-trailers, including integration into legitimate cargo loads, use of refrigerated compartments, and exploitation of expedited trusted-traveler or trusted-shipper lanes. Collectors should be attentive to any indicators of novel concealment engineering or adaptation of techniques previously associated with other contraband types (e.g., currency or weapons smuggling) now being repurposed for fentanyl transport. The intelligence community has long recognized that TCOs are highly adaptive organizations; therefore, collection should also specifically target any anticipated or observed shifts in smuggling routes, corridor preferences, or tradecraft modifications that these organizations may adopt in direct response to heightened U.S. border security posture, increased inspection rates, or new detection technologies deployed at POEs. This includes potential diversion to lesser-used ports of entry, shifts toward maritime or aerial smuggling modalities, or increased use of cross-border tunnel infrastructure. Any intelligence suggesting route migration—for example, from the Tijuana-San Diego corridor to the Nogales-Tucson corridor or vice versa—should be flagged as high priority.

**2. Upstream Precursor Chemical Sourcing Networks:**
A dedicated collection thread must be established focused on upstream precursor chemical sourcing networks that feed the Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG fentanyl production operations. Of particular interest are any ties to suppliers based in the People's Republic of China (PRC) who have been active in this trade since at least 2020. This time-bound requirement reflects the period during which U.S. government reporting and open-source research have documented a significant expansion of PRC-based chemical companies and brokers facilitating the sale and shipment of fentanyl precursors—including 4-ANPP, NPP, and various novel analogues designed to circumvent scheduling controls—to Mexican TCO-affiliated laboratories. Collection should seek to identify specific PRC-based entities, individuals, financial facilitators, and logistics networks involved in precursor supply, including any use of transshipment points in third countries (e.g., India, Guatemala, or countries in Southeast Asia) designed to obscure the origin of chemical shipments. Additionally, collectors should report on any evidence of shifts in precursor sourcing—such as movement toward domestically produced or regionally sourced precursors within Latin America—that might indicate PRC supply chains are being disrupted or diversified.

**3. Assessment of Synthetic Opioid Overdose Fatality Decline:**
CDC provisional data has indicated a roughly one-third decline in synthetic opioid overdose fatalities through October 2024. While this is an encouraging public health development, the intelligence community must help policymakers understand the causal drivers behind this trend. There is a plausible hypothesis that this decline is linked, at least in part, to the dramatically expanded availability and distribution of naloxone (Narcan) and other opioid antagonists, which would represent improved harm reduction on the demand side rather than any meaningful disruption of the fentanyl supply chain. Conversely, it is possible that law enforcement interdiction efforts, precursor chemical scheduling actions, or internal TCO operational disruptions have genuinely reduced the volume or potency of fentanyl reaching U.S. markets. The collection requirement should therefore incorporate specific indicators and diagnostic intelligence questions designed to help analysts assess which of these explanatory frameworks—supply disruption versus demand-side harm reduction—more accurately accounts for the observed decline, or whether the reality involves a combination of both factors. Relevant indicators might include: changes in wholesale and retail fentanyl pricing in U.S. drug markets (price increases would suggest supply constriction); changes in seizure volumes and purity levels at the border and within the U.S. interior; reporting on TCO production tempo and laboratory activity levels in Mexico; and any TCO internal communications reflecting concern about supply chain difficulties or market saturation.

**4. Platform Nomination and Interagency Coordination:**
Nominate all relevant collection platforms across HUMINT, SIGINT, and OSINT disciplines. For HUMINT, this should include both unilateral CIA sources and jointly managed assets, as well as any foreign partner HUMINT reporting streams that may have access to TCO leadership, logistics coordinators, or precursor chemical brokers. For SIGINT, nominate relevant telephony and digital communication intercept capabilities, including any coverage of encrypted messaging platforms known to be favored by TCO operatives. For OSINT, leverage social media monitoring, commercial shipping and trade databases, dark web marketplace analysis, and publicly available chemical industry trade data to supplement classified collection. All platform nominations should include an assessment of expected reporting timelines and collection confidence levels.

Coordination with Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) liaisons is mandatory for deconfliction purposes. This coordination must occur prior to the activation of any new HUMINT tasking to ensure that collection activities do not inadvertently compromise ongoing DEA investigations, CBP enforcement operations, or joint task force activities along the southwest border. Deconfliction should also extend to any FBI counterintelligence equities related to PRC-linked precursor networks.

**5. Deliverable and Timeline:**
The full collection plan—including clearly articulated priority intelligence requirements (PIRs), nominated sources and platforms with justification for each nomination, expected reporting cadences, and defined reporting timelines—must be submitted to the division chief by close of business (COB) Friday. This deadline is firm, as the division chief requires adequate time for review, annotation, and any necessary revisions before the collection plan is forwarded to the National HUMINT Requirements Tasking Center (NHRTC) for formal validation and tasking authority. Ensure the plan is formatted in accordance with current NHRTC submission standards and includes all required metadata fields.
